name: abseil (absl::flat_hash_map, Swiss tables)
workload: uint64_t- and std::string-keyed maps, 1-2 million entries; build+destroy, find, churn (erase+insert), and iterate ops measured via unordered_dense's third-party benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: u64 keys: 4.25x faster build+destroy (18.50ns vs 78.66ns/op), 2.43x faster find (23.82ns vs 57.89ns/op), 3.52x faster churn (68.23ns vs 240.49ns/op), 8.28x faster iterate (2.57ns vs 21.29ns/op) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages (madvise), process pinned to one core, Fedora 44
stars_or_usage: 18.1k stars; used in Chromium, TensorFlow, and widely at Google
tradeoffs: SwissTable open addressing gives no pointer/reference stability on rehash or erase, unlike std::unordered_map's node-based stability; resident memory is roughly on par with std (CSV 'rss' row: absl 1.11x vs std 0.94x-1.06x depending on metric).
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party harness (unordered_dense project's scripts/ab), not abseil's own repo; ratios computed by dividing the CSV's ns/op figures for the 'absl' and 'std' rows on the same page (marked derived). Standard-library implementation (libstdc++ vs libc++) is not explicitly named, only 'clang 22.1.8'. Abseil release tested was LTS 20250814, not necessarily current HEAD.

name: folly F14 (F14ValueMap)
workload: uint64_t- and std::string-keyed maps, 1-2 million entries; build+destroy, find, churn, iterate ops measured via unordered_dense's third-party benchmark harness, F14ValueMap variant specifically.
claimed_speedup: u64 keys: 2.81x faster build+destroy (27.98ns vs 78.66ns/op), 1.72x faster find (33.58ns vs 57.89ns/op), 2.63x faster churn (91.34ns vs 240.49ns/op), 16.35x faster iterate (1.30ns vs 21.29ns/op) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages (madvise), process pinned to one core, Fedora 44
stars_or_usage: 30.5k stars; used extensively in Meta/Facebook production C++ services
tradeoffs: F14ValueMap stores values inline so it lacks std::unordered_map's iterator/reference stability on rehash; F14NodeMap is the stability-preserving variant, at a speed cost; three storage policies plus F14FastMap auto-selector add API/tuning surface versus a single std::unordered_map.
caveats: Folly commit tested was a specific snapshot (65749da), not necessarily current HEAD. F14ValueMap was the variant benchmarked, not F14FastMap (the docs' recommended default) or F14NodeMap (the closer drop-in replacement). Ratios derived by dividing CSV ns/op values for 'f14-value' and 'std' rows on the same page. Standard-library implementation not explicitly named.

name: Boost.Unordered (boost::unordered_flat_map)
workload: uint64_t- and std::string-keyed maps, 1-2 million entries; build+destroy, find, churn, iterate ops measured via unordered_dense's third-party benchmark harness.
claimed_speedup: u64 keys: 3.54x faster build+destroy (22.23ns vs 78.66ns/op), 2.70x faster find (21.42ns vs 57.89ns/op), 4.66x faster churn (51.57ns vs 240.49ns/op), 11.61x faster iterate (1.84ns vs 21.29ns/op) (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages (madvise), process pinned to one core, Fedora 44
stars_or_usage: 92 stars on the standalone module repo; ships inside Boost proper (used far more broadly than the module repo's own star count reflects)
tradeoffs: unordered_flat_map is open-addressed, so no pointer/reference stability across insert/erase, unlike Boost's own node-based boost::unordered_map or std::unordered_map; requires reasonably modern C++ (11+).
caveats: Boost version tested was 1.90. Ratios derived by dividing CSV ns/op values for 'boost' and 'std' rows on the same page. stars_or_usage reflects only the small boostorg/unordered submodule repo, not Boost's overall install base. Standard-library implementation not explicitly named.

name: ankerl::unordered_dense
workload: uint64_t- and std::string-keyed maps, 1-2 million entries; build+destroy, find, churn, iterate ops (own doc/benchmarks.md and scripts/ab harness).
claimed_speedup: u64 keys: 3.50x faster build+destroy (ratio 3.5016, 22.46ns vs 78.66ns/op), 1.98x faster find (ratio 1.9763), 2.84x faster churn (ratio 2.8417); iterate 0.19ns/element vs std::unordered_map's 21.29ns/element ('std::unordered_map needs 110x' per page text)
compiler_and_flags: clang 22.1.8, -O3, transparent huge pages (madvise), process pinned to one core, Fedora 44
stars_or_usage: 1.48k stars; used in MySQL, PrusaSlicer and others per doc/users.md
tradeoffs: No reference/iterator stability on insert or erase (elements live in a std::vector, so growth or erase can move everything); erase is relatively slow (needs two lookups); loses to boost::unordered_flat_map on integer find (0.73x of boost's time) and churn (0.61x) despite winning iteration and string build/destroy.
caveats: This is a first-party benchmark (project's own doc/scripts-ab harness) authored by the same person who wrote the library, but it states compiler, flags, hardware, and publishes the raw CSV and harness script, meeting the tier-A bar on methodology transparency ('the project's own repo... qualif[ies]' per instructions) despite being first-party. Standard-library implementation not explicitly named.

name: robin_hood::unordered_map
workload: README claims faster/leaner performance than std::unordered_map across insert, find and iterate workloads; points to the author's own multi-library 'Hashmap Benchmarks' series (construction, insertion, random find, iteration) for evidence, but that series presents results as chart images rather than text/tables.
claimed_speedup: "robin_hood is always among the fastest maps and uses far less memory than std::unordered_map" (verbatim README claim; no numeric ratio was extractable from the linked benchmark pages via available tooling)
compiler_and_flags: g++ 8.2.0, -O3 -march=native, CMake Release build (stated on the benchmark-series overview page, not in the robin-hood-hashing repo itself)
hardware: Intel Core i7-8700 @ 3.20GHz, locked to 3200MHz (per benchmark-series overview page)
tradeoffs: robin_hood::unordered_flat_map has no reference/pointer stability; robin_hood::unordered_node_map trades speed for that stability via a custom bulk allocator; author has since stopped development and recommends ankerl::unordered_dense as the successor.
caveats: Repo is archived and abandoned since 2023 (author redirects users to unordered_dense). Capped at tier C because the linked benchmark series states full methodology (code, compiler, flags, CPU) but its actual result numbers are rendered as chart images that could not be read as text/data through available tools, so no verified numeric ratio could be quoted. The qualitative README claim itself is a first-party, no-methodology statement.
